anatomy.lede: Seen from below, the peregrine is all purpose: long pointed wings, a compact barred body, a dark 'moustache' and eyes built to lock on to flying birds.

hotspots.label: Bill
hotspots.text: Peregrines usually kill with the bill, by severing the prey's neck vertebrae.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Peregrines have extraordinarily keen vision, able to spot small objects at great distances.

hotspots.label: Cheek stripe
hotspots.text: A black stripe runs down each cheek of the otherwise pale face.

hotspots.label: Barred underparts
hotspots.text: Adults are finely barred below. Females are typically 15–20% larger than males.

hotspots.label: Feet
hotspots.text: In a stoop the falcon closes its feet and uses them to knock prey out of the sky. Even as nestlings, peregrines have very large feet for their size.

hotspots.label: Pointed wing
hotspots.text: To stoop, the falcon folds these long wings and falls into a nose dive.

stats.label: How much heavier females are than males

senses.lede: A peregrine's world is mostly visual: it must find a bird far away, then keep it in sight at very high speed.

senses.name: Distant sight
senses.text: Peregrines have extraordinarily keen vision and hunt by spotting prey from high vantage points.

senses.name: Sideways sharp spot
senses.text: A peregrine's sharpest vision lies about 40° to one side of its head. Holding its head straight while diving, it curves its flight path to keep prey in that sharp spot.

body.lede: Speed is only part of the story. Peregrine bodies are also shaped by how they kill and how the two sexes share the work.

systems.title: Knock, then bite
systems.text: The falcon strikes prey with closed feet, often in mid-air, then kills it with a bite to the neck. Prey may be eaten in flight or stored for later.

systems.title: Bigger females
systems.text: Females are 15–20% larger and 40–50% heavier than males. Simulations suggest males are better at catching very agile prey in level flight, while females can carry up to 50% heavier loads.

systems.title: Bird-eating specialist
systems.text: Birds make up 77–99% of prey items, from starlings and pigeons to shorebirds and ducks; a few peregrines specialise in bats.

genome.lede: The peregrine was one of the first birds of prey to have its genome sequenced, alongside the saker falcon, in 2013.

findings.title: Fast-evolving genomes
findings.text: Comparing about 8,400 genes with those of chicken, turkey and zebra finch showed that falcon genomes have evolved rapidly across the board.

findings.title: Beaks and smell
findings.text: Falcons showed distinctive changes in genes linked to beak development and to smell, which the authors relate to their predatory lifestyle.

findings.title: Fused chromosomes
findings.text: Most birds have about 80 chromosomes, but the peregrine has 50. Chromosome painting shows that many small chromosomes have fused with larger ones in falcons.

mind.lede: Cameras and GPS loggers carried by falcons have shown that their attacks follow surprisingly precise rules.

studies.title: Steering like a missile
studies.text: Footage from falcon-mounted cameras and GPS showed that peregrines close on targets using the same guidance rule as most guided missiles: turning in proportion to how fast the line of sight to the target swings round.

studies.title: Why stoop?
studies.text: Computer simulations suggest a high, fast dive raises catch success against erratically dodging prey, because speed gives the falcon more force to manoeuvre. The best-performing settings matched what real peregrines do.

studies.title: Sky dances
studies.text: Courting pairs perform power dives, tight turns, high soaring and rolls, and gently grip each other's bills at the nest ledge.

survival.lede: Even a peregrine has enemies, especially when young, and its recovery from pesticides is one of conservation's great successes.

tactics.title: Height is an advantage
tactics.text: Peregrines usually hunt from a high perch, which gives them more height from which to begin a stoop.

tactics.title: Many ways to hunt
tactics.text: Besides diving, peregrines chase prey in level flight, sometimes hunt in pairs, and have been seen using ships as perches to hunt seabirds far out at sea.

threats.title: Pesticides still in use
threats.text: Organochlorine pesticides such as DDT and dieldrin thin eggshells. They are restricted in North America but not everywhere in Central and South America, where many peregrines spend the winter.

life.lede: Peregrines grow up fast: a chick can fly about six weeks after hatching.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays 2 to 6 eggs about two days apart. She does most of the incubating.

stages.name: Nestling
stages.text: Chicks are fed by their parents until they are fully feathered and fledge at five to six weeks old.

stages.name: Fledgling
stages.text: After fledging, young falcons stay near their parents while learning to hunt, becoming independent after about six weeks.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females first breed at 1 to 5 years old; males start later, at 2 to 8 years.

lifespan.value: Wild records of 16–20 years; 25 years in captivity
